LANGUAGE BORROWING: ETYMOLOGY AND CHANGES IN MEANING AND PRONUNCIATION OF ARABIC VOCABULARY IN SWAHILI. When speakers of two languages come into contact and interact, those languages can directly borrow from and influence each other phonologically, lexically, and grammatically. When the Arabs arrived on the East African coast, they encountered the Swahili, and it was then that Swahili borrowed words and sounds from Arabic that did not previously exist in the Swahili language. Secondly, Swahili also adopted some Arabic sounds and modified the way they are pronounced. This article investigates and identifies the etymology of certain Arabic words found in the Swahili language and examines how Arabic sounds were borrowed, altered, and adapted into Swahili. Furthermore, it explores how the original meanings of some words changed after being borrowed from Arabic. Theoretical frameworks and cognitive semantics of vocabulary were applied. Introduction:- When Swahili came into contact with the Arabic language, it borrowed two things. It borrowed many Arabic words and adapted them, and secondly, it borrowed Arabic sounds that came with some of those words. The entry of Arabic words and sounds into the Swahili language resulted in two types of language change. The first type of change is the transformation or simplification of Arabic sounds so they can be pronounced by speakers of Swahili, which is a Bantu language. Secondly, there was a change in the original meaning of some Arabic words when they were incorporated into the Swahili language. This article will discuss language borrowing from Arabic into Swahili, the ways in which sound changes took place, and the alteration of the original meaning of some Arabic words borrowed into Swahili. This article employs two theories. The first is the structural theory, which deals with the changes in the sounds of words borrowed from the Arabic language. According to Mulder and Hervy (1975), this theory regards language as a large system comprised of many subsystems within it. They state that language is a system with five subsystems: semantics, pragmatics, syntax. Morphology and phonology. This article will focus on phonology, examining how sounds change. The second theory is that of cognitive lexical semantics. According to Paradis (2012), this theory deals with changes in meaning in words, which is one of the topics of this article. Hamisi Babusa. Address: Kenyatta University. Sound changes in borrowed Arabic words. Many Arabic words borrowed into the Swahili language, in addition to undergoing changes to adapt vowel patterns and conform to the structure of Swahili words, also experienced alterations to their original sounds. These sounds were changed because they did not exist at all in Swahili, and even if they had been borrowed directly, they would have caused pronunciation difficulties for Swahili speakers who were not accustomed to articulating these Arabic sounds. The following examples illustrate the changes in pronunciation of some Arabic words that have been incorporated into the Swahili language. Differentiation Between the Arabic ي (Yee) and the Swahili Vowel. The Arabic ي (Yee) or /y/ is the final consonant in the Arabic alphabet. There are some Arabic words that have a (yee) with a shadda. For example, MANIYYI منێ, NABIYYI نبێ, HAYYU حێ, TWAYYIB ﻄﯿﺐ, and MAYYITU مێټ. When these words were borrowed into Swahili, the ي (yee) was dropped and replaced by the vowel /i/. MANIYYI became MANII, NABIYYI became NABII. HAYYU became HAI, TWAYYIB became taib, MAYYITU became MAITI, etc.

Differentiation of the Arabic ع (‘Ain) and the Swahili Vowel

ﻉ (‘ain) is the eighteenth consonant in the Arabic alphabet. Some Arabic words that contain this sound include: ‘Aib عﯿﺐ, Mu‘allim معلم, ‘Ahdi عﻬد, ‘aqli عﻘل, and tis'a ﺗﺴعﺔ. When these words were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, the Arabic ﻉ ‘ain, which is difficult for Africans to pronounce, was dropped and replaced with a vowel. For example, ‘aib became AIBU, mu’allim became MWALIMU, ‘ahdi became AHADI, ‘aqli became AKILI, and tis’a became TISA.

Change of ﻄ (Twee) in Arabic to /T/ in Swahili

Another sound change occurs where an Arabic word containing the ﻄ (twee) consonant is changed to /t/ after being borrowed into Swahili. For example, the following words are from Arabic: TWAYYIB ﻄﯿﺐ and TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ. When these words were borrowed and incorporated into the Swahili language, the ﻂ (twee) consonant was dropped and replaced with /t/, resulting in the Swahili words TARIKI and TAIB.

Change of ﺺ (Swaad) in Arabic to /S/ in Swahili

Arabic words that have the ﺺ (swaad) consonant, when entering the Swahili language, are changed so that ﺺ (swaad) becomes /s/. For example: SWAADIQ ﺻﺎدﻖ changed to SADIKI, SWAGHYR ﺻﻐﯿﺭ changed to SAGHIRI, and SWIRAAT ﺻﺮﺁﺖ changed to SIRATI.

Change of ﻖ (Qaaf) in Arabic to /K/ in Swahili

In the Arabic alphabet, there is ﻙ (kaaf) /k/ and ﻖ (qaaf). ﻖ (qaaf) is the twenty-first consonant in the Arabic alphabet, pronounced further back in the mouth than /k/, i.e., with contact at the soft palate and the back of the tongue. Bantu speakers did not have this sound, and when words with this Arabic sound were borrowed into Swahili, ﻖ (qaaf) was changed to /k/. For example: SWAADIQ ﺻﺎدﻖ became SADIKI, TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ became TARIKI, ‘AQLI عﻘل became AKILI, WARAQA ﻮﺭﻗﻪ became WARAKA, and WAQTI ﻮﻗﺖ became WAKATI.

Change of ﻇ (Dhwee) in Arabic to /Dh/ in Swahili

ﻇ (dhwee) is the seventeenth letter in the Arabic alphabet. When words containing this sound were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, ﻇ (dhwee) was replaced by /dh/. For example: DHWAALIM ﺂلﻡﻇ became DHALIMU, and NADHWIIF نﻈﯿﻒ became NADHIFU.

Dropping of Arabic Vowels in Swahili

In some Arabic words, there is a prolonged sound or two vowels. When borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, one of the vowels is dropped, leaving only one. For example: TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ changed to become TARIKI, DHWAALIM ﻇﺂلﻡ changed to become DHALIMU, NADHWIIF نﻈﯿﻒ changed to become NADHIFU. Change of ﺽ ('Ddwad) from Arabic to /Dh/ in Swahili: ﺽ ('Ddwad) is the fifteenth consonant in the Arabic alphabet. Most experts classify this sound as /d/, but it is not /d/. It is a sound articulated with the front part of the tongue (not the tip) and the teeth. This sound poses a challenge to pronounce, especially for speakers who are not familiar with the Arabic language. The Swahili do not have this sound, so they looked for a similar one and found /dh/, and immediately words with ﺽ ('llwad) in Arabic changed and began to be pronounced with /dh/ after being incorporated into the Swahili language. An example is: AR'LLI ﺃﺮﺾ changes to become ARDHI; 'LLAR ABUROHD B n ﺮkn an k an ﺐﺮﺿDH. Change in /H/ That Is Voiced and /H/ That Is Unvoiced In the Arabic language, there are two types of /h/. The first is ﺡ /h/ unvoiced and is pronounced from the upper part of the throat. Then there is ﻫ /h/ that is voiced and is pronounced from the chest. In the Swahili language, there is only one /h/, which is pronounced in the throat. Those Arabic words containing the sound /h/ ﻫ that is voiced, when borrowed into the Swahili language, this sound is changed to an unvoiced /h/. for example: “AHDI عﻬد changed to become AHADI, JUHDI ﺠﻫد… The Dropping of Final Sounds in Arabic Words Some Arabic words have final sounds that are often used as suffixes at the end of the word and are usually ﺀ (hamza) and ﺓ /t/. for example: HAYAAI ﺤﻳﺎﺀ, the hamza is dropped and a vowel following /y/ is also removed, so the word changes to HAYA. SWADAQAATU ﺼدﻗﺎﺕ, the final /t/ is dropped and a vowel after /q/ is removed, /qaaf/ becomes /k/, and the word changes to SADAKA. RISAALATU ﺮﺴﺎلﺔ, the final /t/ is dropped and a vowel after /s/ is removed, so the word changes to RISALA. WARAQATU ﻮﺭﻗﺔ, the final /t/ is dropped and /qaaf/ becomes /k/, so the word changes to WARAKA. Transfer of Arabic Word Structures into Swahili: Swahili words are usually arranged in a CV-CV (consonant-vowel) structure. for example, KAKA, DADA, MAMA, etc. Most Arabic words, when borrowed, generally do not follow this pattern of the Swahili language. They usually have the structure CVCCV, etc. However, when they are borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, they are supplied with vowels and changed to follow the CV-CV structure. For example:
‘AHDI (CVCCV) عﻬد changed to become AHADI (VCVCV), JUHDI (CVCVCV) ﺠﻫد became JUHUDI (CVCVCVCV). However, there are some words that retained their Arabic structure when borrowed into Swahili, thereby introducing a new word structure into the Swahili language from Arabic. For example: AR’LLI ﺃﺮﺾ (VCCV) becomes ARDHI (VCCV), KHAMSIIN ﺨﻤﺴﯿﻦ (CVCVCCVC) — when this word was borrowed into Swahili, it retained its original Arabic structure, but underwent a few changes, namely, /kh/ changed to /h/, a vowel immediately after /s/ was dropped, and a vowel was added to the end of the word. But no vowel was inserted after /m/, so the Arabic structure was preserved as it entered Swahili and the word became HAMSINI (CVCVCVCV).

Changes in meaning for some of the borrowed Arabic words.
Most Arabic words borrowed and incorporated into Swahili retained their original meaning from Arabic. However, some words changed meaning after being borrowed and acquired new meanings in the Swahili language. This section will examine some words whose meanings changed following borrowing.

Dari is a Swahili word borrowed from Arabic ﺪﺍﺭ (dār). The original Arabic meaning of this word is HOUSE (NYUMBA), as seen in the phrase ﺪﺍﺭﺴﻼﻡ DĀR SALĀM meaning HOUSE OF PEACE. When borrowed into Swahili, however, its meaning changed—it no longer referred to a 'house' but rather to the upper part of a house, just below the roof.

Alhamisi is a Swahili word borrowed from the Arabic word ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs). According to the Arabic weekly calendar, Alkhamiis is the fifth day. But in Swahili, it is the sixth day of the week. Let us compare the days of the week in Arabic and Swahili:

Jumamosi (first day of the week)      ﻴﻮﻡﺍﻠﺴﺑﺖ (yaumu sabt)    the day of rest
Jumapili (second day of the week)     ﻳﻭﻢﺍﻷﺤﺪ (yaumul-ahad)  the first day of the week
Jumatatu (third day of the week)      ﻳﻭﻡﺍﻹﺜﻧﻴﻦ (yaumul-ithnayn)  the second day of the week
Jumanne (fourth day of the week)      ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺜﻸﺘﺎﺀ (yaumu thulāthā')  the third day of the week
Jumatano (fifth day of the week)      ﺀﻭﻢﺍﻷﺮﺑﻌﺎﺀ (yaumul-arba'ā')   the fourth day of the week

According to the comparison between Swahili and Arabic days, it is clear that the days do not align: the first day in Swahili (Jumamosi) in Arabic is the day of rest, and the second day in Swahili is the first day of the week in Arabic, and so forth. Swahili borrowed two words, ALHAMISI and IJUMAA, from Arabic. However, the word ALHAMISI—which meant ‘the fifth day’ in Arabic—when it entered the Swahili language, its meaning changed to ‘the sixth day of the week.’

Sakafu is a Swahili word borrowed from the Arabic ﺴﻘﻒ (saqf). In Arabic, saqf means CEILING, that is, the upper part of a house beneath the roof. However, when this word was borrowed into Swahili, its meaning changed to refer to the lower part of the house—that which is laid and cemented.

Nahau is another word borrowed from the Arabic ﺍﻟنﺤﻭ (an-nahwu), which originally means GRAMMAR in Arabic. However, when incorporated into Swahili, the word took on a new meaning: a group of words that together carry a special meaning not directly derived from the usual meanings of the individual words. Linguistics is a word that was also borrowed from the Arabic language ﺍﻹﺴﻡ (al-ismu), whose original meaning is NAME. When this word was borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, its meaning changed to refer to the discipline that studies and scientifically analyzes language. Waraka was also borrowed from the Arabic language ﻮﺭﻗﺔ (waraqatu). The original meaning of this word in Arabic is LEAF OF A TREE. However, when it was borrowed and incorporated into the Swahili language, its meaning changed to refer to documents written on a piece of paper that convey certain information. In conclusion, this article examines and analyzes the various phonological changes of Arabic words that were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili. After identifying various changes, it was determined that many Arabic words were adapted into Swahili after being borrowed, with their consonants altered to simplify pronunciation for Bantu speakers. In addition, there are sounds and pronunciation patterns that were borrowed directly from Arabic without any modification. Moreover, there were also changes in meaning in some of the borrowed Arabic words incorporated into the Swahili language. Therefore, the evidence shows that both changes in meaning and pronunciation occurred in some Swahili words borrowed from Arabic. References:- 1. Khamisi A. B. Utangulizi:- Kiswahili kilipogusana na lugha ya Kiarabu, kilikopa vitu viwili. Iliazima maneno mengi ya Kiarabu na kuyarekebisha, na pili, iliazima sauti za Kiarabu zilizokuja na baadhi ya maneno hayo. Kuingia kwa maneno na sauti za Kiarabu katika lugha ya Kiswahili kulisababisha aina mbili za mabadiliko ya lugha. Aina ya kwanza ya mabadiliko ni ugeuzaji au kurahisisha sauti za Kiarabu ili ziweze kutamkwa na wazungumzaji wa Kiswahili ambacho ni lugha ya Kibantu. Pili, kulikuwa na mabadiliko katika maana asilia ya baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu yalipoingizwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili. Makala haya yatazungumzia ukopaji wa lugha kutoka Kiarabu hadi Kiswahili, njia ambazo mabadiliko ya sauti yalifanyika, na ubadilishaji wa maana asilia ya baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa kwa Kiswahili. Makala haya yanatumia nadharia mbili. Ya kwanza ni nadharia ya umuundo, inayohusu mabadiliko ya sauti za maneno yaliyokopwa kutoka lugha ya Kiarabu. Kwa mujibu wa Mulder na Hervy (1975), nadharia hii inaichukulia lugha kuwa mfumo mkubwa unaojumuisha tanzu nyingi ndani yake. Wanasema kuwa lugha ni mfumo wenye mifumo midogo mitano: semantiki, pragmatiki, sintaksia. Mofolojia na fonolojia. Makala haya yatajikita zaidi katika fonolojia, tukichunguza jinsi sauti zinavyobadilika. Nadharia ya pili ni ile ya semantiki ya kileksia tambuzi. Kwa mujibu wa Paradis (2012), nadharia hii inahusu mabadiliko ya maana katika maneno, ambayo ni mada mojawapo ya makala haya. Hamisi Babusa. Anwani: Chuo Kikuu cha Kenyatta. Mabadiliko ya sauti katika maneno ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa. Maneno mengi ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili, pamoja na kufanyiwa mabadiliko ya kurekebisha mifumo ya vokali na kuendana na muundo wa maneno ya Kiswahili, pia yalipata mabadiliko ya sauti zao asilia. Sauti hizi zilibadilishwa kwa sababu hazikuwepo kabisa katika Kiswahili, na hata zingeazimwa moja kwa moja, zingesababisha matatizo ya kimatamshi kwa wazungumzaji wa Kiswahili ambao hawakuwa na mazoea ya kutamka sauti hizi za Kiarabu. Mifano ifuatayo inadhihirisha mabadiliko ya matamshi ya baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu ambayo yamejumuishwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili. Tofauti Kati ya Kiarabu ي (Yee) na Vokali ya Kiswahili. Kiarabu ي (Yee) au /y/ ni konsonanti ya mwisho katika alfabeti ya Kiarabu. Kuna baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu yana (yee) yenye shadda. Kwa mfano, mimi ni MWANAUME, mimi si Nabii, ni MWANAZUONI, ni MWANAMKE na ni MWANAMKE. Maneno haya yalipokopwa kwa Kiswahili, ي (yee) ilidondoshwa na nafasi yake kuchukuliwa na vokali /i/. NYUMBA ikawa NYUMBA, NABII akawa NABII. HAYYU akawa HAI, TWAYYIB akawa taib, MAYYITU akawa MAJI, nk.

Utofautishaji wa Kiarabu ع (‘Ain) na Vokali ya Kiswahili

ع (‘ain) ni konsonanti ya kumi na nane ya alfabeti ya Kiarabu. Baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu ambayo yana sauti hii ni pamoja na: 'Aib 'Aib, Mu'allim Mu'allim, 'Ahdi 'Ad, 'Aqli 'Al, na 'Tis'a Tasa'at. Maneno haya yalipokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili, ع 'ain ya Kiarabu, ambayo ni vigumu kwa Waafrika kuitamka, iliangushwa na badala yake kuwekwa vokali. Kwa mfano, ‘aib akawa AIBU, mu’allim akawa MWALIMU, ‘ahdi akawa AHADI, ‘aqli akawa AKILI, na tis’a akawa TISA.

Mabadiliko ya /Twee katika Kiarabu hadi /T/ kwa Kiswahili

Badiliko jingine la sauti hutokea pale neno la Kiarabu lenye konsonanti ع (twee) hubadilishwa na kuwa /t/ baada ya kuazima kwa Kiswahili. Kwa mfano, maneno yafuatayo yametoka kwa Kiarabu: TWAYYIB YIB na TWAARIQ ررح. Maneno haya yalipokopwa na kuingizwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili, konsonanti ل (twee) iliondolewa na nafasi yake kuchukuliwa na /t/ na kusababisha maneno ya Kiswahili TARIKI na TAIB.

Kubadilishwa kwa س (Swaad) katika Kiarabu hadi /S/ kwa Kiswahili

Kuna aina nyingi tofauti za konsonanti s (swaad) katika lugha ya Kiswahili. Kwa mfano: SWADIQ ADD ilibadilishwa hadi SADIKI, SWAGYR AKIR ilibadilishwa hadi SAGHIRI, na SWIRAAT RAT ilibadilishwa hadi SIRATI.

Mabadiliko ya /K/ katika Kiarabu hadi /K/ kwa Kiswahili

Katika alfabeti ya Kiarabu, kuna ل (kaaf) /k/ na ع (qaaf). ؖ (qaaf) ni konsonanti ishirini na moja katika alfabeti ya Kiarabu, inayotamkwa nyuma zaidi mdomoni kuliko /k/, yaani, kwa kugusana kwenye kaakaa laini na nyuma ya ulimi. Wazungumzaji wa Kibantu hawakuwa na sauti hii, na maneno yenye sauti hii ya Kiarabu yalipokopwa kwa Kiswahili, ؖ (qaaf) ilibadilishwa kuwa /k/. Kwa mfano: SWADIQ HADIT ikawa SADIKI, TWAARIQ RAR ikawa HISTORIA, ‘AQLI عل ikawa AKILI, WARAQA URQA ikawa WARAKA, na WAQTI WAQT ikawa TIME.

Mabadiliko ya /Dh/ katika Kiarabu hadi /Dh/ kwa Kiswahili

ل (dhwee) ni herufi ya kumi na saba ya alfabeti ya Kiarabu. Maneno yenye sauti hii yalipokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili, l (dhwee) ilibadilishwa na /dh/. Kwa mfano: DHWAALIM اللمة akawa DHALIMU, na NADHWIIF NAYIB akawa NADHIFU.

Kushuka kwa Vokali za Kiarabu katika Kiswahili

Katika baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu, kuna sauti ndefu au vokali mbili. Inapokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili, vokali moja hutupwa na kubaki moja tu. Kwa mfano: TWAARIQ ررح ilibadilishwa kuwa TARIKI, DHWAALIM اللم ilibadilishwa hadi DHALIMU, NADHWIIF نييب imebadilishwa hadi DHWAALIM. Mabadiliko ya . SWADAQAATU SADAKAAT, mwisho /t/ hudondoshwa na vokali baada ya /q/ kuondolewa, /qaaf/ huwa /k/, na neno hubadilika na kuwa SADAKA. RISAALATU RISALA, mwisho /t/ hudondoshwa na vokali baada ya /s/ huondolewa, hivyo neno hubadilika na kuwa RISALA. WARAQATU ni neno, mwisho /t/ hudondoshwa na /qaaf/ huwa /k/, hivyo neno hubadilika na kuwa WARAKA. Uhamisho wa Miundo ya Maneno ya Kiarabu kwa Kiswahili: Maneno ya Kiswahili kwa kawaida hupangwa katika muundo wa CV-CV (konsonanti-vokali). kwa mfano, KAKA, DADA, MAMA n.k. Maneno mengi ya Kiarabu yanapokopwa kwa ujumla hayafuati mtindo huu wa lugha ya Kiswahili. Kawaida huwa na muundo wa CVCCV, nk. Hata hivyo, zinapoazimwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili, hutolewa kwa vokali na kubadilishwa kufuata muundo wa CV-CV. Kwa mfano:
‘AHDI (CVCCV) عﻬد ilibadilika na kuwa AHADI (VVCCV), JUHDI (CVCVCV) ﺠﻫد ikawa JUHUDI (CVCVCVCV). Hata hivyo, kuna baadhi ya maneno ambayo yalidumisha muundo wake wa Kiarabu yalipokopwa kwa Kiswahili, na hivyo kuingiza muundo mpya wa maneno katika lugha ya Kiswahili kutoka Kiarabu. Kwa mfano: AR’LLI ﺃﺮﺾ (VCCV) inakuwa ARDHI (VCCV), KHAMSIIN ﺨﻤﺴﯿﻦ (CVCVCCVC) — neno hili lilipokopwa kwa Kiswahili, lilihifadhi muundo wake asilia wa Kiarabu, lakini lilifanyiwa mabadiliko machache, yaani, /kh/ vokali iliongezwa mara moja baada ya/h/ mwisho wa neno. Lakini hakuna vokali iliyoingizwa baada ya /m/, hivyo muundo wa Kiarabu ulihifadhiwa ulipoingia Kiswahili na neno hilo likawa HAMSINI (CVCVCVCV).

Mabadiliko ya maana kwa baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa.
Maneno mengi ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili yalihifadhi maana yake asilia kutoka Kiarabu. Hata hivyo, baadhi ya maneno yalibadilika maana baada ya kukopwa na kupata maana mpya katika lugha ya Kiswahili. Sehemu hii itachunguza baadhi ya maneno ambayo maana zake zilibadilika kufuatia kuazima.

Dari ni neno la Kiswahili lililokopwa kutoka kwa Kiarabu ﺪﺍﺭ (dār). Maana asili ya Kiarabu ya neno hili ni NYUMBA (NYUMBA), kama inavyoonekana katika maneno ﺪﺍﺭﺴﻼﻡ DĀR SALĀM yenye maana ya NYUMBA YA AMANI. Hata hivyo, ilipoazimwa katika Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika—haikurejelea tena ‘nyumba’ bali sehemu ya juu ya nyumba, chini kidogo ya paa.

Alhamisi ni neno la Kiswahili lililokopwa kutoka kwa neno la Kiarabu ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs). Kulingana na kalenda ya kila wiki ya Kiarabu, Alkhamiis ni siku ya tano. Lakini kwa Kiswahili ni siku ya sita ya juma. Hebu tulinganishe siku za wiki kwa Kiarabu na Kiswahili:

Kiswahili Kiarabu
Jumamosi (siku ya kwanza ya juma) ﻴﻮﻡﺍﻠﺴﺑﺖ (yaumu sabt) siku ya mapumziko
Jumapili (siku ya pili ya juma) ﻳﻭﻢﺍﻷﺤﺪ (yaumul-ahad) siku ya kwanza ya juma
Jumatatu (siku ya tatu ya juma) ﻳﻭﻡﺍﻹﺜﻧﻴﻦ (yaumul-ithnayn) siku ya pili ya juma
Jumanne (siku ya nne ya juma) ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺜﻸﺘﺎﺀ (yaumu thulathā') siku ya tatu ya juma
Jumatano (siku ya tano ya juma) ﺀﻭﻢﺍﻷﺮﺑﻌﺎﺀ (yaumul-arba'ā') siku ya nne ya juma
Alhamisi (siku ya sita ya juma) ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs) siku ya tano ya juma
Ijumaa (siku ya kukamilisha wiki) ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺟﻤﻌﺔ (yaumul-jumu‘a) siku ya mwisho ya juma.

Kwa mujibu wa ulinganisho wa siku za Kiswahili na Kiarabu, ni wazi kwamba siku hazilingani: siku ya kwanza katika Kiswahili (Jumamosi) kwa Kiarabu ni siku ya mapumziko, na siku ya pili katika Kiswahili ni siku ya kwanza ya juma kwa Kiarabu, na kadhalika. Waswahili waliazima maneno mawili, ALHAMISI na IJUMAA, kutoka Kiarabu. Hata hivyo, neno ALHAMISI—ambalo lilimaanisha ‘siku ya tano’ katika Kiarabu—lilipoingia katika lugha ya Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika na kuwa ‘siku ya sita ya juma.

Sakafu ni neno la Kiswahili lililokopwa kutoka kwa Kiarabu ﺴﻘﻒ (saqf). Kwa Kiarabu, saqf ina maana ya dari, yaani, sehemu ya juu ya nyumba iliyo chini ya paa. Hata hivyo, neno hili lilipokopwa kwa Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika na kurejelea sehemu ya chini ya nyumba—iliyowekwa na kuwekewa saruji.

Nahau ni neno lingine lililokopwa kutoka kwa Kiarabu ﺍﻟنﺤﻭ (an-nahwu), ambalo asili yake linamaanisha SARUFI katika Kiarabu. Hata hivyo, neno hilo lilipoingizwa katika Kiswahili, lilipata maana mpya: kikundi cha maneno ambacho kwa pamoja hubeba maana maalum isiyotokana moja kwa moja na maana za kawaida za maneno binafsi. Isimu ni neno ambalo pia lilikopwa kutoka lugha ya Kiarabu ﺍﻹﺴﻡ (al-ismu), ambalo maana yake asilia ni JINA. Neno hili lilipokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika na kurejelea taaluma inayochunguza na kuichambua lugha kisayansi. Waraka pia iliazimwa kutoka lugha ya Kiarabu ﻮﺭﻗﺔ (waraqatu). Maana asili ya neno hili kwa Kiarabu ni JANI LA ​​MTI. Hata hivyo, ilipoazimwa na kuingizwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika na kurejelea hati zilizoandikwa kwenye kipande cha karatasi zinazowasilisha habari fulani. Kwa kumalizia, makala haya yanachunguza na kuchambua mabadiliko mbalimbali ya kifonolojia ya maneno ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili. Baada ya kubainisha mabadiliko mbalimbali, ilibainika kuwa maneno mengi ya Kiarabu yalitolewa katika Kiswahili baada ya kuazima, huku konsonanti zake zikibadilishwa ili kurahisisha matamshi kwa wazungumzaji wa Kibantu. Kwa kuongezea, kuna sauti na mifumo ya matamshi ambayo ilikopwa moja kwa moja kutoka kwa Kiarabu bila marekebisho yoyote. Zaidi ya hayo, pia kulikuwa na mabadiliko ya maana katika baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa yaliyoingizwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili. Kwa hiyo, ushahidi unaonyesha kwamba mabadiliko yote mawili katika maana na matamshi yalitokea katika baadhi ya maneno ya Kiswahili yaliyokopwa kutoka Kiarabu. Marejeleo:- 1. Khamisi A. B. discourses.source_txt: When the Arabs arrived on the East African coast, they encountered the Swahili, and it was then that Swahili borrowed words and sounds from Arabic that did not previously exist in the Swahili language. Secondly, Swahili also adopted some Arabic sounds and modified the way they are pronounced. This article investigates and identifies the etymology of certain Arabic words found in the Swahili language and examines how Arabic sounds were borrowed, altered, and adapted into Swahili. Furthermore, it explores how the original meanings of some words changed after being borrowed from Arabic.

discourses.source_txt: …………………………………………………………………………………………………….... Introduction:- When Swahili came into contact with the Arabic language, it borrowed two things. It borrowed many Arabic words and adapted them, and secondly, it borrowed Arabic sounds that came with some of those words. The entry of Arabic words and sounds into the Swahili language resulted in two types of language change. The first type of change is the transformation or simplification of Arabic sounds so they can be pronounced by speakers of Swahili, which is a Bantu language. Secondly, there was a change in the original meaning of some Arabic words when they were incorporated into the Swahili language. This article will discuss language borrowing from Arabic into Swahili, the ways in which sound changes took place, and the alteration of the original meaning of some Arabic words borrowed into Swahili. This article employs two theories. The first is the structural theory, which deals with the changes in the sounds of words borrowed from the Arabic language. According to Mulder and Hervy (1975), this theory regards language as a large system comprised of many subsystems within it. They state that language is a system with five subsystems: semantics, pragmatics, syntax.

discourses.source_txt: Sound changes in borrowed Arabic words. Many Arabic words borrowed into the Swahili language, in addition to undergoing changes to adapt vowel patterns and conform to the structure of Swahili words, also experienced alterations to their original sounds. These sounds were changed because they did not exist at all in Swahili, and even if they had been borrowed directly, they would have caused pronunciation difficulties for Swahili speakers who were not accustomed to articulating these Arabic sounds. The following examples illustrate the changes in pronunciation of some Arabic words that have been incorporated into the Swahili language.

Differentiation of the Arabic ع (‘Ain) and the Swahili Vowel

ﻉ (‘ain) is the eighteenth consonant in the Arabic alphabet. Some Arabic words that contain this sound include: ‘Aib عﯿﺐ, Mu‘allim معلم, ‘Ahdi عﻬد, ‘aqli عﻘل, and tis'a ﺗﺴعﺔ. When these words were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, the Arabic ﻉ ‘ain, which is difficult for Africans to pronounce, was dropped and replaced with a vowel. For example, ‘aib became AIBU, mu’allim became MWALIMU, ‘ahdi became AHADI, ‘aqli became AKILI, and tis’a became TISA.

Change of ﻄ (Twee) in Arabic to /T/ in Swahili

Another sound change occurs where an Arabic word containing the ﻄ (twee) consonant is changed to /t/ after being borrowed into Swahili. For example, the following words are from Arabic: TWAYYIB ﻄﯿﺐ and TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ. When these words were borrowed and incorporated into the Swahili language, the ﻂ (twee) consonant was dropped and replaced with /t/, resulting in the Swahili words TARIKI and TAIB.

Change of ﺺ (Swaad) in Arabic to /S/ in Swahili

Arabic words that have the ﺺ (swaad) consonant, when entering the Swahili language, are changed so that ﺺ (swaad) becomes /s/. For example: SWAADIQ ﺻﺎدﻖ changed to SADIKI, SWAGHYR ﺻﻐﯿﺭ changed to SAGHIRI, and SWIRAAT ﺻﺮﺁﺖ changed to SIRATI.

Change of ﻖ (Qaaf) in Arabic to /K/ in Swahili

In the Arabic alphabet, there is ﻙ (kaaf) /k/ and ﻖ (qaaf). ﻖ (qaaf) is the twenty-first consonant in the Arabic alphabet, pronounced further back in the mouth than /k/, i.e., with contact at the soft palate and the back of the tongue. Bantu speakers did not have this sound, and when words with this Arabic sound were borrowed into Swahili, ﻖ (qaaf) was changed to /k/. For example: SWAADIQ ﺻﺎدﻖ became SADIKI, TWAARIQ ﻄﺂﺮﻖ became TARIKI, ‘AQLI عﻘل became AKILI, WARAQA ﻮﺭﻗﻪ became WARAKA, and WAQTI ﻮﻗﺖ became WAKATI.

Change of ﻇ (Dhwee) in Arabic to /Dh/ in Swahili

ﻇ (dhwee) is the seventeenth letter in the Arabic alphabet. When words containing this sound were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, ﻇ (dhwee) was replaced by /dh/. For example: DHWAALIM ﺂلﻡﻇ became DHALIMU, and NADHWIIF نﻈﯿﻒ became NADHIFU.

Dropping of Arabic Vowels in Swahili

In some Arabic words, there is a prolonged sound or two vowels. When borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, one of the vowels is dropped, leaving only one.

Utofautishaji wa Kiarabu ع (‘Ain) na Vokali ya Kiswahili

ع (‘ain) ni konsonanti ya kumi na nane ya alfabeti ya Kiarabu. Baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu ambayo yana sauti hii ni pamoja na: 'Aib 'Aib, Mu'allim Mu'allim, 'Ahdi 'Ad, 'Aqli 'Al, na 'Tis'a Tasa'at. Maneno haya yalipokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili, ع 'ain ya Kiarabu, ambayo ni vigumu kwa Waafrika kuitamka, iliangushwa na badala yake kuwekwa vokali. Kwa mfano, ‘aib akawa AIBU, mu’allim akawa MWALIMU, ‘ahdi akawa AHADI, ‘aqli akawa AKILI, na tis’a akawa TISA.

Mabadiliko ya /Twee katika Kiarabu hadi /T/ kwa Kiswahili

Badiliko jingine la sauti hutokea pale neno la Kiarabu lenye konsonanti ع (twee) hubadilishwa na kuwa /t/ baada ya kuazima kwa Kiswahili. Kwa mfano, maneno yafuatayo yametoka kwa Kiarabu: TWAYYIB YIB na TWAARIQ ررح. Maneno haya yalipokopwa na kuingizwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili, konsonanti ل (twee) iliondolewa na nafasi yake kuchukuliwa na /t/ na kusababisha maneno ya Kiswahili TARIKI na TAIB.

Kubadilishwa kwa س (Swaad) katika Kiarabu hadi /S/ kwa Kiswahili

Kuna aina nyingi tofauti za konsonanti s (swaad) katika lugha ya Kiswahili. Kwa mfano: SWADIQ ADD ilibadilishwa hadi SADIKI, SWAGYR AKIR ilibadilishwa hadi SAGHIRI, na SWIRAAT RAT ilibadilishwa hadi SIRATI.

Mabadiliko ya /K/ katika Kiarabu hadi /K/ kwa Kiswahili

Katika alfabeti ya Kiarabu, kuna ل (kaaf) /k/ na ع (qaaf). ؖ (qaaf) ni konsonanti ishirini na moja katika alfabeti ya Kiarabu, inayotamkwa nyuma zaidi mdomoni kuliko /k/, yaani, kwa kugusana kwenye kaakaa laini na nyuma ya ulimi. Wazungumzaji wa Kibantu hawakuwa na sauti hii, na maneno yenye sauti hii ya Kiarabu yalipokopwa kwa Kiswahili, ؖ (qaaf) ilibadilishwa kuwa /k/. Kwa mfano: SWADIQ HADIT ikawa SADIKI, TWAARIQ RAR ikawa HISTORIA, ‘AQLI عل ikawa AKILI, WARAQA URQA ikawa WARAKA, na WAQTI WAQT ikawa TIME.

Mabadiliko ya /Dh/ katika Kiarabu hadi /Dh/ kwa Kiswahili

ل (dhwee) ni herufi ya kumi na saba ya alfabeti ya Kiarabu. Maneno yenye sauti hii yalipokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili, l (dhwee) ilibadilishwa na /dh/. Kwa mfano: DHWAALIM اللمة akawa DHALIMU, na NADHWIIF NAYIB akawa NADHIFU.

Kushuka kwa Vokali za Kiarabu katika Kiswahili

Katika baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu, kuna sauti ndefu au vokali mbili. Inapokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili, vokali moja hutupwa na kubaki moja tu.

Change in /H/ That Is Voiced and /H/ That Is Unvoiced In the Arabic language, there are two types of /h/. The first is ﺡ /h/ unvoiced and is pronounced from the upper part of the throat. Then there is ﻫ /h/ that is voiced and is pronounced from the chest.
discourses.translated_txt: Mfano ni: AR'LLI ﺃﺮﺾ hubadilika na kuwa ARDHI; 'LLAR ABUROHD B n ﺮkn an k an ﺐﺮﺿDH. Badiliko katika /H/ Inayotamkwa na /H/ Isiyotamkwa Katika lugha ya Kiarabu, kuna aina mbili za /h/. Ya kwanza ni ﺡ /h/ isiyotamkwa na hutamkwa kutoka sehemu ya juu ya koo. Kisha kuna ﻫ /h/ ambayo hutamkwa na hutamkwa kutoka kifuani.

discourses.source_txt: In the Swahili language, there is only one /h/, which is pronounced in the throat.
discourses.translated_txt: Katika lugha ya Kiswahili, kuna /h/ moja tu, ambayo hutamkwa kooni.

discourses.source_txt: Those Arabic words containing the sound /h/ ﻫ that is voiced, when borrowed into the Swahili language, this sound is changed to an unvoiced /h/.
discourses.translated_txt: Maneno hayo ya Kiarabu yenye sauti /h/ ﻫ inayotamkwa, yanapokopwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili, sauti hii hubadilishwa na kuwa /h/ isiyotamkwa.

SWADAQAATU ﺼدﻗﺎﺕ, the final /t/ is dropped and a vowel after /q/ is removed, /qaaf/ becomes /k/, and the word changes to SADAKA. Transfer of Arabic Word Structures into Swahili: Swahili words are usually arranged in a CV-CV (consonant-vowel) structure.

discourses.source_txt:
For example:
‘AHDI (CVCCV) عﻬد changed to become AHADI (VCVCV), JUHDI (CVCVCV) ﺠﻫد became JUHUDI (CVCVCVCV). However, there are some words that retained their Arabic structure when borrowed into Swahili, thereby introducing a new word structure into the Swahili language from Arabic. For example: AR’LLI ﺃﺮﺾ (VCCV) becomes ARDHI (VCCV), KHAMSIIN ﺨﻤﺴﯿﻦ (CVCVCCVC) — when this word was borrowed into Swahili, it retained its original Arabic structure, but underwent a few changes, namely, /kh/ changed to /h/, a vowel immediately after /s/ was dropped, and a vowel was added to the end of the word. But no vowel was inserted after /m/, so the Arabic structure was preserved as it entered Swahili and the word became HAMSINI (CVCVCVCV).

Changes in meaning for some of the borrowed Arabic words.
Most Arabic words borrowed and incorporated into Swahili retained their original meaning from Arabic. However, some words changed meaning after being borrowed and acquired new meanings in the Swahili language. This section will examine some words whose meanings changed following borrowing.

Dari is a Swahili word borrowed from Arabic ﺪﺍﺭ (dār). The original Arabic meaning of this word is HOUSE (NYUMBA), as seen in the phrase ﺪﺍﺭﺴﻼﻡ DĀR SALĀM meaning HOUSE OF PEACE. When borrowed into Swahili, however, its meaning changed—it no longer referred to a 'house' but rather to the upper part of a house, just below the roof.

Alhamisi is a Swahili word borrowed from the Arabic word ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs). According to the Arabic weekly calendar, Alkhamiis is the fifth day. But in Swahili, it is the sixth day of the week. Let us compare the days of the week in Arabic and Swahili:

Swahili               Arabic
Jumamosi (first day of the week)      ﻴﻮﻡﺍﻠﺴﺑﺖ (yaumu sabt)    the day of rest
Jumapili (second day of the week)     ﻳﻭﻢﺍﻷﺤﺪ (yaumul-ahad)  the first day of the week
Jumatatu (third day of the week)      ﻳﻭﻡﺍﻹﺜﻧﻴﻦ (yaumul-ithnayn)  the second day of the week
Jumanne (fourth day of the week)      ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺜﻸﺘﺎﺀ (yaumu thulāthā')  the third day of the week
Jumatano (fifth day of the week)      ﺀﻭﻢﺍﻷﺮﺑﻌﺎﺀ (yaumul-arba'ā')   the fourth day of the week
Alhamisi (sixth day of the week)      ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs)      the fifth day of the week
Ijumaa (day of completing the week)   ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺟﻤﻌﺔ (yaumul-jumu‘a)     the last day of the week

According to the comparison between Swahili and Arabic days, it is clear that the days do not align: the first day in Swahili (Jumamosi) in Arabic is the day of rest, and the second day in Swahili is the first day of the week in Arabic, and so forth. Swahili borrowed two words, ALHAMISI and IJUMAA, from Arabic. However, the word ALHAMISI—which meant ‘the fifth day’ in Arabic—when it entered the Swahili language, its meaning changed to ‘the sixth day of the week.’

Sakafu is a Swahili word borrowed from the Arabic ﺴﻘﻒ (saqf). In Arabic, saqf means CEILING, that is, the upper part of a house beneath the roof. However, when this word was borrowed into Swahili, its meaning changed to refer to the lower part of the house—that which is laid and cemented.

Nahau is another word borrowed from the Arabic ﺍﻟنﺤﻭ (an-nahwu), which originally means GRAMMAR in Arabic. However, when incorporated into Swahili, the word took on a new meaning: a group of words that together carry a special meaning not directly derived from the usual meanings of the individual words.
discourses.translated_txt:
Kwa mfano:
‘AHDI (CVCCV) عﻬد ilibadilika na kuwa AHADI (VVCCV), JUHDI (CVCVCV) ﺠﻫد ikawa JUHUDI (CVCVCVCV). Hata hivyo, kuna baadhi ya maneno ambayo yalidumisha muundo wake wa Kiarabu yalipokopwa kwa Kiswahili, na hivyo kuingiza muundo mpya wa maneno katika lugha ya Kiswahili kutoka Kiarabu. Kwa mfano: AR’LLI ﺃﺮﺾ (VCCV) inakuwa ARDHI (VCCV), KHAMSIIN ﺨﻤﺴﯿﻦ (CVCVCCVC) — neno hili lilipokopwa kwa Kiswahili, lilihifadhi muundo wake asilia wa Kiarabu, lakini lilifanyiwa mabadiliko machache, yaani, /kh/ vokali iliongezwa mara moja baada ya/h/ mwisho wa neno. Lakini hakuna vokali iliyoingizwa baada ya /m/, hivyo muundo wa Kiarabu ulihifadhiwa ulipoingia Kiswahili na neno hilo likawa HAMSINI (CVCVCVCV).

Mabadiliko ya maana kwa baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa.
Maneno mengi ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili yalihifadhi maana yake asilia kutoka Kiarabu. Hata hivyo, baadhi ya maneno yalibadilika maana baada ya kukopwa na kupata maana mpya katika lugha ya Kiswahili. Sehemu hii itachunguza baadhi ya maneno ambayo maana zake zilibadilika kufuatia kuazima.

Dari ni neno la Kiswahili lililokopwa kutoka kwa Kiarabu ﺪﺍﺭ (dār). Maana asili ya Kiarabu ya neno hili ni NYUMBA (NYUMBA), kama inavyoonekana katika maneno ﺪﺍﺭﺴﻼﻡ DĀR SALĀM yenye maana ya NYUMBA YA AMANI. Hata hivyo, ilipoazimwa katika Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika—haikurejelea tena ‘nyumba’ bali sehemu ya juu ya nyumba, chini kidogo ya paa.

Alhamisi ni neno la Kiswahili lililokopwa kutoka kwa neno la Kiarabu ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs). Kulingana na kalenda ya kila wiki ya Kiarabu, Alkhamiis ni siku ya tano. Lakini kwa Kiswahili ni siku ya sita ya juma. Hebu tulinganishe siku za wiki kwa Kiarabu na Kiswahili:

Kiswahili Kiarabu
Jumamosi (siku ya kwanza ya juma) ﻴﻮﻡﺍﻠﺴﺑﺖ (yaumu sabt) siku ya mapumziko
Jumapili (siku ya pili ya juma) ﻳﻭﻢﺍﻷﺤﺪ (yaumul-ahad) siku ya kwanza ya juma
Jumatatu (siku ya tatu ya juma) ﻳﻭﻡﺍﻹﺜﻧﻴﻦ (yaumul-ithnayn) siku ya pili ya juma
Jumanne (siku ya nne ya juma) ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺜﻸﺘﺎﺀ (yaumu thulathā') siku ya tatu ya juma
Jumatano (siku ya tano ya juma) ﺀﻭﻢﺍﻷﺮﺑﻌﺎﺀ (yaumul-arba'ā') siku ya nne ya juma
Alhamisi (siku ya sita ya juma) ﺃﻠﺧﻤﻴﺱ (alkhamīs) siku ya tano ya juma
Ijumaa (siku ya kukamilisha wiki) ﻴﻭﻢﺍﻟﺟﻤﻌﺔ (yaumul-jumu‘a) siku ya mwisho ya juma.

Kwa mujibu wa ulinganisho wa siku za Kiswahili na Kiarabu, ni wazi kwamba siku hazilingani: siku ya kwanza katika Kiswahili (Jumamosi) kwa Kiarabu ni siku ya mapumziko, na siku ya pili katika Kiswahili ni siku ya kwanza ya juma kwa Kiarabu, na kadhalika. Waswahili waliazima maneno mawili, ALHAMISI na IJUMAA, kutoka Kiarabu. Hata hivyo, neno ALHAMISI—ambalo lilimaanisha ‘siku ya tano’ katika Kiarabu—lilipoingia katika lugha ya Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika na kuwa ‘siku ya sita ya juma.

Sakafu ni neno la Kiswahili lililokopwa kutoka kwa Kiarabu ﺴﻘﻒ (saqf). Kwa Kiarabu, saqf ina maana ya dari, yaani, sehemu ya juu ya nyumba iliyo chini ya paa. Hata hivyo, neno hili lilipokopwa kwa Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika na kurejelea sehemu ya chini ya nyumba—iliyowekwa na kuwekewa saruji.

Nahau ni neno lingine lililokopwa kutoka kwa Kiarabu ﺍﻟنﺤﻭ (an-nahwu), ambalo asili yake linamaanisha SARUFI katika Kiarabu. Hata hivyo, neno hilo lilipoingizwa katika Kiswahili, lilipata maana mpya: kikundi cha maneno ambacho kwa pamoja hubeba maana maalum isiyotokana moja kwa moja na maana za kawaida za maneno binafsi.

discourses.source_txt: Linguistics is a word that was also borrowed from the Arabic language ﺍﻹﺴﻡ (al-ismu), whose original meaning is NAME. When this word was borrowed and incorporated into Swahili, its meaning changed to refer to the discipline that studies and scientifically analyzes language.
discourses.translated_txt: Isimu ni neno ambalo pia lilikopwa kutoka lugha ya Kiarabu ﺍﻹﺴﻡ (al-ismu), ambalo maana yake asilia ni JINA. Neno hili lilipokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika na kurejelea taaluma inayochunguza na kuichambua lugha kisayansi.

discourses.source_txt: Waraka was also borrowed from the Arabic language ﻮﺭﻗﺔ (waraqatu). The original meaning of this word in Arabic is LEAF OF A TREE.
discourses.translated_txt: Waraka pia iliazimwa kutoka lugha ya Kiarabu ﻮﺭﻗﺔ (waraqatu). Maana asili ya neno hili kwa Kiarabu ni JANI LA ​​MTI.

discourses.source_txt: However, when it was borrowed and incorporated into the Swahili language, its meaning changed to refer to documents written on a piece of paper that convey certain information. In conclusion, this article examines and analyzes the various phonological changes of Arabic words that were borrowed and incorporated into Swahili.
discourses.translated_txt: Hata hivyo, ilipoazimwa na kuingizwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili, maana yake ilibadilika na kurejelea hati zilizoandikwa kwenye kipande cha karatasi zinazowasilisha habari fulani. Kwa kumalizia, makala haya yanachunguza na kuchambua mabadiliko mbalimbali ya kifonolojia ya maneno ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa na kuingizwa katika Kiswahili.

discourses.source_txt: After identifying various changes, it was determined that many Arabic words were adapted into Swahili after being borrowed, with their consonants altered to simplify pronunciation for Bantu speakers. In addition, there are sounds and pronunciation patterns that were borrowed directly from Arabic without any modification. Moreover, there were also changes in meaning in some of the borrowed Arabic words incorporated into the Swahili language. Therefore, the evidence shows that both changes in meaning and pronunciation occurred in some Swahili words borrowed from Arabic.
discourses.translated_txt: Baada ya kubainisha mabadiliko mbalimbali, ilibainika kuwa maneno mengi ya Kiarabu yalitolewa katika Kiswahili baada ya kuazima, huku konsonanti zake zikibadilishwa ili kurahisisha matamshi kwa wazungumzaji wa Kibantu. Kwa kuongezea, kuna sauti na mifumo ya matamshi ambayo ilikopwa moja kwa moja kutoka kwa Kiarabu bila marekebisho yoyote. Zaidi ya hayo, pia kulikuwa na mabadiliko ya maana katika baadhi ya maneno ya Kiarabu yaliyokopwa yaliyoingizwa katika lugha ya Kiswahili. Kwa hiyo, ushahidi unaonyesha kwamba mabadiliko yote mawili katika maana na matamshi yalitokea katika baadhi ya maneno ya Kiswahili yaliyokopwa kutoka Kiarabu.
